summary: GalaxyCore is a free, offline-ready web app that teaches children aged 6–12 about the machines humanity left on the Moon and Mars. Instead of forgetting these explorers, kids recover their stories: an interactive 3D globe places eight explorers (Apollo 11 Eagle, ALSEP, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Lunokhod 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and InSight) at their real coordinates, with color-coded status (still working, partly in use, out of service). Each explorer has a case file told in the first person across five moments (birth, journey, mission, last day, legacy), with voice narration, verified facts and a short "recovery mission" quiz. Four of them can also be played: 16 levels, many in real-time 3D, recreate real events such as the Apollo lunar landing, Opportunity's "hole-in-one" landing and the 2018 dust storm, and Spirit driving backwards with a broken wheel. The project turns NASA mission history into curiosity, empathy and science learning for young Spanish-speaking students in Peru.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

GalaxyCore is a Spanish-language educational web app for children aged 6–12. It combines an "explorer memorial" with playable missions:

1) Ghosts of Space – Explorer Map: a rotating 3D globe of the Moon and Mars (procedurally generated textures with real features such as Mare Tranquillitatis, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris and Hellas). Eight explorers sit at their real landing coordinates, colored by current status. Each has a case file with: a first-person story in 5 moments (birth, journey, mission, last day, legacy) with text-to-speech; a fact sheet (dates, site, distance, coordinates); "What did we learn?" discoveries; and a 3-question "Recovery Mission". Recovered explorers are tracked (x/8). The app states clearly that the voices are imagined but the facts are real.

2) Playable missions (16 levels):

- Lunar Roving Vehicle / Apollo 15: first-person Lunar Module landing seen through the window; driving the rover to Spur crater to find the "Genesis Rock"; and remotely operating the rover's TV camera from Houston with real signal delay.

- Lunokhod 2: remote driving with signal delay, lunar day/night survival, photo planning and the laser retroreflector still used today.

- Spirit (3D): entry, descent and landing with airbags; rock analysis; driving backwards with a stuck wheel that uncovered silica; and the sand trap at Troy.

- Opportunity (3D): "hole-in-one" landing in Eagle crater; hematite "blueberries"; solar power with dust devils; and the 2018 global dust storm.

3) Home: a 3D Moon, Earth and Mars with a guide robot (Bip), real relative-size comparison, gravity and jump comparison, a robot collection and progress tracking.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Turns NASA mission history into stories children can relate to (persistence, teamwork, how missions end) while teaching science: water on Mars, moonquakes and marsquakes, solar power, gravity.

- Works offline once loaded, with no accounts and no data collection (local progress only). Suited to Peruvian schools with limited connectivity.

- Accessibility: voice narration, a reduced-motion "calm mode", an optional "more data" mode for ages 9–12, a parents/teachers panel, and adaptive 3D quality for low-end devices.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, Vite, three.js (WebGL 3D: procedural terrain, sky shaders, shadows, particles), GSAP (animation), Web Audio API (sound), Web Speech API (narration), localStorage (progress), Playwright (automated testing). All planet, terrain and explorer graphics are procedurally generated or hand-drawn SVG by the team; no NASA logos or images are embedded.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a quiz about rovers, kids meet each machine as a character who tells its own story and "recover" it, then live key moments of its real mission through game mechanics based on actual events.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Age-appropriate reading level and short sessions; factual accuracy checked against NASA sources; clear separation between fiction (voice) and fact; international explorers included (Lunokhod 2, USSR, shown as an international guest); performance on low-cost hardware; offline use; child privacy.

LANGUAGES

The app is bilingual (Spanish / English) with a one-tap language switch.

SI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE) DISCLOSURE

- Code and text: parts of the source code and educational texts were developed with the assistance of an SI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) and reviewed and verified by the team against NASA sources.

- Video: the lunar module landing clip used in the app intro and in the demo is marked on screen as "SI-GENERATED FOOTAGE".

- Audio: the demo's background music and sound effects were generated by code with SI assistance; the voice-over was recorded by our team.

- No NASA logos, insignia or branding are used in the app or the demo.
